newsitem.title: USA: Argentine economy basically strong - Camdessus.
newsitem.headline: Argentine economy basically strong - Camdessus.

text.p: Argentina's economy is basically strong but its government must complete decisive reforms, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus said Thursday.
"Argentina is truly on its way to entering the new century on a very, very solid basis," Camdessus said at a news conference held ahead of next week's joint meeting of the IMF and the World Bank.
However, Camdessus said Argentina had yet to complete its structural reforms and grapple with pervasive corruption.

"Argentina is already playing in the world's first class league of strong economies (but) you can't stay there or prosper there if you don't get rid of the corruption factor and if you don't generally improve governance," he said.
Camdessus pointed out that corruption was a problem all over the world, adding that Argentine authorities were committed to fight it.
He added that governments that undertake structural reforms also have to be ready to face up to vested interests, such as trade unions that oppose measures to introduce flexibility in job markets.
Argentina's trade unions started Thursday a 36-hour nationwide strike against the economic programs of President Carlos Menem, who has derided the protest as a lame excuse for a long weekend.

Camdessus argued that one of the keys to solving Argentina's record unemployment rate, which under Menem has grown to 17 percent of the workforce, was to "reduce the privileges of those who have jobs for the benefits of those who do not have jobs".
According to the IMF chief, the reforms Argentina launched in 1991 produced its best economic results in over 60 years.

"Argentina has made great progress towards the in-depth modernization of its economic structure, it got rid of inflation and it has availed itself with a currency which is as good as the dollar," he added.
Argentina's peso is linked to the dollar by a 1991 law that established a currency board, under which its central bank must back the local currency with U.S. dollars, gold or government bonds.
